### In Praise of the Wrong Turn

There is a street near the edge of my childhood that I can still walk down, though I could not draw it accurately on a map. It begins beside a row of shops with metal shutters and ends, I think, near a railway bridge, though the bridge may have come down years ago. In between are a bakery that smells of cardamom, a house with a blue door, an empty lot where weeds grow with almost architectural precision, and a cat who regards everyone with professional suspicion.

According to the map, this street should take fifteen minutes to cross.

On foot, it takes an afternoon.

I have always liked that arithmetic. Distance is not only measured in miles; it is measured in willingness. The bakery might require a second visit. The blue door might belong to someone who knows a story about the house next to it. The cat might eventually decide that I am harmless. Plans are useful, but they are poor poets: they tell us where we are going without much imagination about what we might meet.

Modern navigation promises certainty. Tap a blue line and the world arranges itself around you. If you miss a turn, a calm electronic voice offers to recalculate. Yet there is something faintly suspicious about a journey in which nothing is ever lost. If you never take the wrong road, you may never discover that the road was a village with a pond, or a hill with a view, or a shortcut that only exists in winter.

Children understand this instinctively—or perhaps they understand it before adulthood teaches them to be efficient. A walk to the park can become an expedition. A missing sock can delay departure. A stick is so compelling that nobody notices the sun has moved and the ordinary walk home has quietly become an adventure.

Getting lost, of course, can be dangerous. The distinction matters. A person lost in a storm needs a map more than a metaphor. But there are smaller kinds of confusion, gentler ones—the feeling of being somewhere without understanding how you arrived. These are not failures of intelligence. They are openings.

When you are following a route, the world is background. When you are lost, the world comes forward. You notice the cracked paving stone shaped like a river. You remember the name of a tree. You realize that the person who gave you directions spoke as if the place were larger than it is, and perhaps it is larger because of everything you would have missed by hurrying through.

This is also true beyond geography. We arrange our lives around destinations: graduation, promotion, marriage, the clean bright line of a future we can describe. Occasionally the wrong turn gives us a year with a new friend, a job we would never have heard of, a morning that changes the direction of our thinking. We call these things diversions, as though they were interruptions in the real business of life. But perhaps they are the point. Perhaps the route was never the point.

Leave some margin in the afternoon. Take the street that does not quite look right. Look at the blue door. Let the journey become, for a little while, unaccountable.

The destination, after all, is only one way to come home.
